The Markdown uses a thin space (U+2009) between numbers and units (e.g. '843 mmol/mol', '0.8‐38 years') and around '<'; spans were copied with that character, escaped as \\u2009. Tables 3 and 4 list metabolite values with no patient label column, so no value was assigned to a person by row position (D-31). Tables 1 and 2 both number patients 1-7; the Table 2 note \"Patients 1 and 2 identical to patients 1 and 2 in Table 1\" shows those are the same people, so the Table-2-only patients are labelled \"Patient N (Table 2)\" to keep labels unique; Tables 3/4 rows correspond to the same 10 newborn DBS (7 patients) and 17 post-newborn patients. 1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency, the disease caused by germline *ALDH5A1* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ssadh_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *ALDH5A1* variant or a diagnosis of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *ALDH5A1* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *ALDH5A1* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;

160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.

168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

1	Extraction rules (GP-RareLink, v1). These rules apply to every table and every row.
2	
3	1. Use only the supplied document. Do not use outside knowledge about the gene, the disease, specific variants or specific patients. If the document does not state something, the value is "not reported" (for text fields) or null (for numeric and date fields). Never fill a gap from memory.
4	2. Every value must be supported by a verbatim quote copied exactly from the document. Do not paraphrase inside the quote. If no exact quote supports a value, do not emit the value.
5	3. Keep original strings. Record variant descriptions, ages, feature names and labels exactly as printed. Never convert protein-only variant descriptions into cDNA notation, never add a transcript that is not printed, never translate units.

8	# Longitudinal metabolomics in dried bloodspots yields profiles informing newborn screening for succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractAnalyses of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) were implemented to test the hypothesis that succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) could be identified in dried bloodspots (DBS) using currently available newborn screening methodology. The study population included 17 post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (age range 0.8‐38 years; median, 8.2 years; 10 M; controls, 129‐353 age‐matched individuals, mixed gender) and 10 newborn SSADHD DBS (including first and second screens from 3 of 7 patients). Low (informative) markers in post‐newborn DBS included C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, ornithine, histidine and creatine, with no gender differences. For newborn DBS, informative markers included C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, creatine and ornithine. Of these, only creatine demonstrated a significant change with age, revealing an approximate 4‐fold decrease. We conclude that quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method for γ‐hydroxybutyric acid in the same DBS. More extensive evaluation of this first/second tier screening approach is needed in a larger population.Keywords: acylcarnitines, amino acids, creatine, dried bloodspots, newborn screening, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency

20	## INTRODUCTION
21	
22	1.
23	
24	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) is a rare genetic disease associated with mutations of the ALDH5A1 gene, tissue accumulation of neuromodulators including γ‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) and γ‐hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), and tissue depletion of glutamine (gln), the precursor of GABA and glutamic acid (glu). SSADHD presents with nonspecific mild to moderate developmental delay, intellectual deficiency, severe expressive language impairment, neuropsychiatric problems (ADHD, obsessive compulsive disorder, autistic behavior), and variable epilepsy.1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 There have been reports of sudden unexplained death of epilepsy9, 10 (Gibson, unpublished).
25	
26	Current approaches and major gaps to patient identification and treatment are summarized in Figure 1. Since SSADHD was first described in 1981, research has focused on identifying the spectrum of pathogenic ALDH5A1 mutations, understanding the molecular and biochemical basis of disease presentation, and testing promising therapeutics. The development of an animal model11 resulted in significant strides in elucidation of pathomechanisms and development of novel preclinical therapeutics, including a recently completed interventional trial with the GABA_BR antagonist SGS‐742 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02019667), as well as a completed open‐label trial of taurine which failed to demonstrate efficacy.12 Treatment for SSADHD remains symptomatic, yet an expanding therapeutic preclinical pipeline strongly suggests that targeted and effective therapies (in addition to vigabatrin, which directly targets GABA metabolism) for SSADHD are on the horizon.13
27

VGB (vigabatrin; γ‐vinylGABA; Sabril) represents an irreversible inhibitor of GABA‐T
29	
30	Implementation of newborn screening (NBS) for SSADHD is clinically important for a number of reasons. Expanded NBS would maximize the therapeutic benefit of targeted therapeutics, facilitate family planning, and remove the potential off‐target effects of commonly used symptomatic agents, effectively constituting “treatment by omission.” Further, NBS could synergize with a recently undertaken natural history study of SSADHD through significant expansion of the span of longitudinal assessment of the disorder. NBS would detect patients who will develop milder forms of the disease, or patients with clinical presentations so subtle that they may be misdiagnosed. The potential for delayed diagnosis is highlighted in the postmortem identification of an adult male in the fifth decade.5 Early patient diagnosis would further serve to refine disease prevalence estimates, increase the pool of patients available for a natural history study and future clinical trials, and provide insight on disease pathogenesis and the genetic factors that track with milder disease presentation.
31	
32	The incidence of SSADHD has been estimated at 1 × 10^6 based upon mutation (allele) frequency (Dr Nilah Monnier, Stanford‐personal communication). Mutation analysis has been available for many years.14 Detection of SSADHD has continued to expand with the addition of ALDH5A1 gene analysis to several commercial epilepsy and intellectual disability panels; however, only ~50% of SSADHD patients have seizures, suggesting that many patients remain undiagnosed. On the other hand, methodology for GHB quantitation in dried bloodspots (DBS) has been presented.15 That method utilized liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry (LC‐MS/MS). At least in the United States, only a very limited number of states employ LC/MS‐MS for metabolite quantification, primarily because it is insufficiently high‐throughput (run time 2‐3 minutes per DBS vs 1 minute with MS/MS alone). States with smaller populations, and an often correspondingly lower birthrate, have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS which can expand their metabolic screening “menu,” but states with larger populations (New York, California, and Texas) may only have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS as a second tier screen, or for very specialized analytical needs. Nonetheless, GHB quantitation in DBS represents a very attractive second tier test for confirmation of SSADHD.
33	
34	Recent surveys of SSADHD families worldwide indicate that the median age at disease onset is 1 year whereas the median age at diagnosis is 3 years, that is, a 2‐year delay after the first clinical symptoms. Under current circumstances (with a median age at diagnosis of 3 years), any natural history study of SSADHD would not include patients diagnosed in the early newborn period, representing a major confound from the neurodevelopmental perspective of a disease manifesting a prominent neurological phenotype. Moreover, these survey data provide a measurable perspective on the disease burden for SSADHD families who have to wait 3 years to achieve a diagnosis, as well as the public health and societal impact of delayed diagnosis. To address these unmet healthcare needs, we examined the hypothesis that an integrated screen of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) could be used to potentially identify a metabolomic pattern that could be used as an first‐tier screening tool for SSADHD using DBS, an approach that has been successful in a number of inborn errors of metabolism.16, 17, 18

93	Analyses of amino acids, acylcarnitines (saturated and unsaturated), and creatine derivatives were performed using tandem mass spectrometry as previously described.18, 24 A single 3 mm punch from one DBS was used. 95	### Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports
96	
97	2.3.
98	
99	Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports (CLIR 2.12; https://clir.mayo.edu) is a web application that maintains an interactive database of laboratory results from multiple sites and provides on demand clinical decision support for their integrated interpretation.25 CLIR replace conventional reference intervals with continuous, covariate‐adjusted moving percentiles,26 as well as replacement of analyte decision limits (ie, cutoff values) with a condition‐specific degree of overlap between reference and disease ranges. Further, an additional feature of CLIR incorporates integration of primary markers and unbiased biomarker discovery by automated calculation of all possible permutations of ratios (A/B) plus manual selection of complex ratios and equations, which can be performed simultaneously for all conditions that can be diagnosed from the available laboratory measurements.

105	Metabolic measures were integrated within CLIR, facilitating comparison with anonymized DBS data from multiple NBS centers throughout the world. Analyte‐covariate analysis employed age as covariate. Gender was known for reference and patient values, but was only assessed as covariate for informative markers in the post‐newborn DBS samples of SSADHD. Statistical analysis included one‐way analysis of variance or two‐tailed t test using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (San Diego, California).

183	## DISCUSSION
184	
185	4.
186	
187	### Comparison of metabolic panels to detect SSADHD in DBS
188	
189	4.1.
190	
191	#### Informative amino acid markers
192	
193	4.1.1.
194	
195	Based upon the known metabolic correlations between glutamine, glutamate, and GABA,27, 28, 29 our initial prediction was glutamic acid and glutamine would serve as informative markers for SSADHD in DBS. These amino acids were, however, noninformative, whereas ornithine and histidine were. Indeed, the most consistent amino acid dysregulation was that of ornithine, both in post‐newborn and newborn DBS. Low ornithine has hitherto not been reported in plasma amino acid analysis of patients with SSADHD. Conversely, ornithine has been implicated in the ocular toxicity associated with vigabatrin, an antiepileptic whose mode of action encompasses irreversible inactivation of GABA‐transaminase (Figure 1) with concomitant elevation of GABA, a finding analogous to that of SSADHD.30 Shank and Campbell31 demonstrated that both orn and gln can serve to replenish glu and GABA pools, although gln has a more prominent role in this process.
196	
197	Of interest, histidine was only informative for post‐newborn DBS and not newborn DBS. It is noteworthy that histidine is conjugated with GABA in CNS to derive the dipeptide homocarnosine, an osmoregulator that is also increased in cerebrospinal fluid of SSADHD patients.32, 33 Nevertheless, we could not document the presence of homocarnosine in post‐newborn SSADHD DBS, perhaps indicating that the enzyme required for GABA‐histidine conjugation is not active in the newborn period.
198	
199	#### Informative acylcarnitine markers
200	
201	4.1.2.
202	
203	Short‐chain acylcarnitine species were informative in both post‐newborn and newborn SSADHD DBS, encompassing C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitine in the post‐newborn samples and C2‐, C3‐, C4‐, and C4‐OH in newborn SSADHD DBS. This may not be surprising in view of the accumulation of both GHB and succinic semialdehyde in SSADHD,13, 34 which may interfere with short chain fatty acid metabolism. This observation is further supported by the early reports of dicarboxylic aciduria and unusual tetronic acid derivatives in SSADHD.22, 35 Depleted levels of acetyl‐carnitine further suggest reduced mitochondrial function, which we and others have observed both in SSADHD and other disorders of fat oxidation.36, 37 Low levels of 3‐hydroxybutyryl‐carnitine may also provide insight into the success of the ketogenic diet in aldh5a1
204	^−/− mice.38 Administration of the ketogenic diet to these animals significantly elevated blood levels of 3‐hydroxybutyrate while significantly improving the phenotype of seizures and runted growth in this model.
205	
206	#### Creatine as an informative marker for SSADHD DBS
207	
208	4.1.3.
209	
210	Creatine was an informative marker in both post‐newborn and newborn SSADHD DBS. Previously, we had documented the presence of 4‐guanidinobutyrate in tissue and physiological fluids of both aldh5a1
211	^−/− mice and patients with SSADHD.39, 40 This species is predicted to derive from conjugation of GABA (in lieu of glycine) in the arginine:glycine amidinotransferase reaction of the creatine biosynthetic pathway. On the other hand, if this pathway is engaged, we might expect depletion of arginine in DBS, which was not an informative amino acid marker in either post‐newborn or newborn SSADHD DBS.
212	
213	#### Utility of metabolomic profiles as a potential 1st tier screen for SSADH deficiency
214	
215	4.1.4.
216	
217	For both newborn and post‐newborn SSADHD DBS, there was a degree of overlap with reference ranges. However, the individual markers taken together may provide a metabolomic profile with a high degree of probability for accurate detection of SSADH deficiency. For example, it is informative to compare the mean values of biomarkers for patients (n = 10; Table 3) in comparison to the 1%ile of the control data range (n = 9840‐5 089 207) (the appropriate data are italicized in Table 3). These results highlight the fact that the patient means are below this control percentile for both ornithine and creatine, and very close to this percentile for the four acylcarnitine species. Accordingly, the newborn profile of C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine in DBS may highlight an informative “biosignature” of SSADH deficiency.
218	
219	For post‐newborn DBS (Table 4), it is similarly informative to compare the mean of patient DBS (n = 17) to the 1%ile of the control DBS (n = 129‐353) for the five biomarkers shown, including orn, his, C2‐ and C4‐OH acylcarnitines, and creatine. For histidine, the mean patient DBS data were below the 1%ile of parallel DBS control data, while the mean C4‐OH for patient DBS is proximal to the parallel 1%ile control DBS data (pertinent data sets in Table 4 are italicized), while the mean for all five biomarkers resides well below the median of control DBS data. The fact that four of six biomarkers show parallel patterns between newborn and post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (ornithine, C2‐ and C4‐OH‐acylcarnitines, and creatine) lends further credence to the idea that this “biosignature” of biomarkers is informative for SSADH deficiency. At this time, and in the absence of specific funding for those studies, retrospective “in silico” analyses of metabolic patients in archival newborn DBS has not been undertaken, but such data will provide key sensitivity and specificity data, as well as predictive value, for the metabolomic profile results we have observed.
220	
221	## LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE STUDIES
222	
223	5.
224	
225	A primary limitation with this study is the low number of both post‐newborn and newborn SSADHD DBS, especially the latter. This issue is compounded by the fact that different states within the USA retain archival NBS DBS for variable times, with some states discarding samples at the end of 1 year, others at 6‐8 years, and still others retaining their samples for decades or indefinitely. This provides inherent challenges in accruing substantial numbers of newborn SSADHD DBS. Moreover, conditions of storage are often variable, with some states storing archival DBS at room temperature, while others may keep these samples at 4°C. For post‐newborn DBS, an additional confound is medication (we did not have information on medication intake for the current study), and the potential influence of medications on DBS metabolites. We plan to significantly expand the number of newborn SSADHD DBS for further evaluation.
226	
227	It remains to be determined if GABA (free, or esterified) can be quantified in human DBS, but at present this analyte is not present on US NBS panels. Moreover, it would be worthwhile to evaluate the current SSADHD DBS for the presence of 4‐guanidinobutyrate, which may be a potentially relevant biomarker for SSADHD, as well as further characterizing the presence/absence of homocarnosine and carnosine (the latter the dipeptide of his and β‐alanine). These might be pertinent to the development of a sensitive first‐tier screen for SSADHD using DBS. A second‐tier screen already exists that can quantify GHB in DBS (see Introduction15, 41) or via mutation analysis.14 Finally, any methodology pertinent to the newborn detection of SSADHD may have relevance to the identification of GABA‐transaminase deficiency,42 as more patients are being identified. With regard the latter, our prediction is that ornithine will remain an informative marker in DBS.
228	
229	## CONCLUSIONS
230	
231	6.
232	
233	Quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier LC‐MS/MS method for GHB in the same DBS. Our approach awaits more extensive evaluation in a larger population.

12	AbstractAnalyses of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) were implemented to test the hypothesis that succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) could be identified in dried bloodspots (DBS) using currently available newborn screening methodology. The study population included 17 post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (age range 0.8‐38 years; median, 8.2 years; 10 M; controls, 129‐353 age‐matched individuals, mixed gender) and 10 newborn SSADHD DBS (including first and second screens from 3 of 7 patients). Low (informative) markers in post‐newborn DBS included C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, ornithine, histidine and creatine, with no gender differences. For newborn DBS, informative markers included C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, creatine and ornithine. Of these, only creatine demonstrated a significant change with age, revealing an approximate 4‐fold decrease. We conclude that quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method for γ‐hydroxybutyric acid in the same DBS. More extensive evaluation of this first/second tier screening approach is needed in a larger population.Keywords: acylcarnitines, amino acids, creatine, dried bloodspots, newborn screening, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency

4	Title: Longitudinal metabolomics in dried bloodspots yields profiles informing newborn screening for succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
5	Journal: JIMD Reports (2020)
6	Authors: Brown Madalyn; Turgeon Coleman; Rinaldo Piero; Pop Ana; Salomons Gajja S; Roullet Jean‐Baptiste; Gibson K Michael
7	
8	# Longitudinal metabolomics in dried bloodspots yields profiles informing newborn screening for succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractAnalyses of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) were implemented to test the hypothesis that succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) could be identified in dried bloodspots (DBS) using currently available newborn screening methodology. The study population included 17 post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (age range 0.8‐38 years; median, 8.2 years; 10 M; controls, 129‐353 age‐matched individuals, mixed gender) and 10 newborn SSADHD DBS (including first and second screens from 3 of 7 patients). Low (informative) markers in post‐newborn DBS included C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, ornithine, histidine and creatine, with no gender differences. For newborn DBS, informative markers included C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, creatine and ornithine. Of these, only creatine demonstrated a significant change with age, revealing an approximate 4‐fold decrease. We conclude that quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method for γ‐hydroxybutyric acid in the same DBS. More extensive evaluation of this first/second tier screening approach is needed in a larger population.Keywords: acylcarnitines, amino acids, creatine, dried bloodspots, newborn screening, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
13	
14	AbbreviationsC2‐carnitineacetyl‐carnitineC4‐OH‐carnitine3‐hydroxybutyryl‐carnitineFfemaleMmale
15	
16	Synopsis
17	
18	Quantitation of ornithine, short‐chain acylcarnitines, and creatine in newborn dried bloodspots may provide a metabolomic profile with potential as an first tier screen for succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency.
19	
20	## INTRODUCTION
21	
22	1.
23	
24	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) is a rare genetic disease associated with mutations of the ALDH5A1 gene, tissue accumulation of neuromodulators including γ‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) and γ‐hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), and tissue depletion of glutamine (gln), the precursor of GABA and glutamic acid (glu). SSADHD presents with nonspecific mild to moderate developmental delay, intellectual deficiency, severe expressive language impairment, neuropsychiatric problems (ADHD, obsessive compulsive disorder, autistic behavior), and variable epilepsy.1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 There have been reports of sudden unexplained death of epilepsy9, 10 (Gibson, unpublished).
25	
26	Current approaches and major gaps to patient identification and treatment are summarized in Figure 1. Since SSADHD was first described in 1981, research has focused on identifying the spectrum of pathogenic ALDH5A1 mutations, understanding the molecular and biochemical basis of disease presentation, and testing promising therapeutics. The development of an animal model11 resulted in significant strides in elucidation of pathomechanisms and development of novel preclinical therapeutics, including a recently completed interventional trial with the GABA_BR antagonist SGS‐742 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02019667), as well as a completed open‐label trial of taurine which failed to demonstrate efficacy.12 Treatment for SSADHD remains symptomatic, yet an expanding therapeutic preclinical pipeline strongly suggests that targeted and effective therapies (in addition to vigabatrin, which directly targets GABA metabolism) for SSADHD are on the horizon.13
27	
28	**Figure 1**: The GABA metabolic pathway (top) and overview of approaches toward patient identification and treatment (bottom). Metabolites elevated in patients with succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency (SSADHD) include GABA, SSA (succinic semialdehyde), and GHB (γ‐hydroxybutyric acid); conversely, glutamine (gln) appears decreased. For the diagram, green indicates procedures or measures either achieved (solid line) or partially achieved/in progress (broken line). A tier 1 (tier 2 = confirmation of initial screen) bloodspot assay that is amenable to current NBS platforms is currently required (red). Additional abbreviations: GLNase, glutaminase; GAD, glutamic acid decarboxylase; GABA‐T, GABA‐transaminase (also referred to as ABAT, or aminobutyrate aminotransferase); SSADH, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase; AKR7a2, aldo‐keto reductase 7a2. VGB (vigabatrin; γ‐vinylGABA; Sabril) represents an irreversible inhibitor of GABA‐T
29	
30	Implementation of newborn screening (NBS) for SSADHD is clinically important for a number of reasons. Expanded NBS would maximize the therapeutic benefit of targeted therapeutics, facilitate family planning, and remove the potential off‐target effects of commonly used symptomatic agents, effectively constituting “treatment by omission.” Further, NBS could synergize with a recently undertaken natural history study of SSADHD through significant expansion of the span of longitudinal assessment of the disorder. NBS would detect patients who will develop milder forms of the disease, or patients with clinical presentations so subtle that they may be misdiagnosed. The potential for delayed diagnosis is highlighted in the postmortem identification of an adult male in the fifth decade.5 Early patient diagnosis would further serve to refine disease prevalence estimates, increase the pool of patients available for a natural history study and future clinical trials, and provide insight on disease pathogenesis and the genetic factors that track with milder disease presentation.
31	
32	The incidence of SSADHD has been estimated at 1 × 10^6 based upon mutation (allele) frequency (Dr Nilah Monnier, Stanford‐personal communication). Mutation analysis has been available for many years.14 Detection of SSADHD has continued to expand with the addition of ALDH5A1 gene analysis to several commercial epilepsy and intellectual disability panels; however, only ~50% of SSADHD patients have seizures, suggesting that many patients remain undiagnosed. On the other hand, methodology for GHB quantitation in dried bloodspots (DBS) has been presented.15 That method utilized liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry (LC‐MS/MS). At least in the United States, only a very limited number of states employ LC/MS‐MS for metabolite quantification, primarily because it is insufficiently high‐throughput (run time 2‐3 minutes per DBS vs 1 minute with MS/MS alone). States with smaller populations, and an often correspondingly lower birthrate, have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS which can expand their metabolic screening “menu,” but states with larger populations (New York, California, and Texas) may only have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS as a second tier screen, or for very specialized analytical needs. Nonetheless, GHB quantitation in DBS represents a very attractive second tier test for confirmation of SSADHD.
33	
34	Recent surveys of SSADHD families worldwide indicate that the median age at disease onset is 1 year whereas the median age at diagnosis is 3 years, that is, a 2‐year delay after the first clinical symptoms. Under current circumstances (with a median age at diagnosis of 3 years), any natural history study of SSADHD would not include patients diagnosed in the early newborn period, representing a major confound from the neurodevelopmental perspective of a disease manifesting a prominent neurological phenotype. Moreover, these survey data provide a measurable perspective on the disease burden for SSADHD families who have to wait 3 years to achieve a diagnosis, as well as the public health and societal impact of delayed diagnosis. To address these unmet healthcare needs, we examined the hypothesis that an integrated screen of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) could be used to potentially identify a metabolomic pattern that could be used as an first‐tier screening tool for SSADHD using DBS, an approach that has been successful in a number of inborn errors of metabolism.16, 17, 18

95	### Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports
96	
97	2.3.
98	
99	Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports (CLIR 2.12; https://clir.mayo.edu) is a web application that maintains an interactive database of laboratory results from multiple sites and provides on demand clinical decision support for their integrated interpretation.25 CLIR replace conventional reference intervals with continuous, covariate‐adjusted moving percentiles,26 as well as replacement of analyte decision limits (ie, cutoff values) with a condition‐specific degree of overlap between reference and disease ranges. Further, an additional feature of CLIR incorporates integration of primary markers and unbiased biomarker discovery by automated calculation of all possible permutations of ratios (A/B) plus manual selection of complex ratios and equations, which can be performed simultaneously for all conditions that can be diagnosed from the available laboratory measurements.

Statistical analysis included one‐way analysis of variance or two‐tailed t test using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (San Diego, California).

183	## DISCUSSION
184	
185	4.
186	
187	### Comparison of metabolic panels to detect SSADHD in DBS
188	
189	4.1.
190	
191	#### Informative amino acid markers
192	
193	4.1.1.
194	
195	Based upon the known metabolic correlations between glutamine, glutamate, and GABA,27, 28, 29 our initial prediction was glutamic acid and glutamine would serve as informative markers for SSADHD in DBS. These amino acids were, however, noninformative, whereas ornithine and histidine were. Indeed, the most consistent amino acid dysregulation was that of ornithine, both in post‐newborn and newborn DBS. Low ornithine has hitherto not been reported in plasma amino acid analysis of patients with SSADHD. Conversely, ornithine has been implicated in the ocular toxicity associated with vigabatrin, an antiepileptic whose mode of action encompasses irreversible inactivation of GABA‐transaminase (Figure 1) with concomitant elevation of GABA, a finding analogous to that of SSADHD.30 Shank and Campbell31 demonstrated that both orn and gln can serve to replenish glu and GABA pools, although gln has a more prominent role in this process.
196	
197	Of interest, histidine was only informative for post‐newborn DBS and not newborn DBS. It is noteworthy that histidine is conjugated with GABA in CNS to derive the dipeptide homocarnosine, an osmoregulator that is also increased in cerebrospinal fluid of SSADHD patients.32, 33 Nevertheless, we could not document the presence of homocarnosine in post‐newborn SSADHD DBS, perhaps indicating that the enzyme required for GABA‐histidine conjugation is not active in the newborn period.

10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractAnalyses of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) were implemented to test the hypothesis that succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) could be identified in dried bloodspots (DBS) using currently available newborn screening methodology. The study population included 17 post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (age range 0.8‐38 years; median, 8.2 years; 10 M; controls, 129‐353 age‐matched individuals, mixed gender) and 10 newborn SSADHD DBS (including first and second screens from 3 of 7 patients). Low (informative) markers in post‐newborn DBS included C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, ornithine, histidine and creatine, with no gender differences. For newborn DBS, informative markers included C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, creatine and ornithine. Of these, only creatine demonstrated a significant change with age, revealing an approximate 4‐fold decrease. We conclude that quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method for γ‐hydroxybutyric acid in the same DBS. More extensive evaluation of this first/second tier screening approach is needed in a larger population.Keywords: acylcarnitines, amino acids, creatine, dried bloodspots, newborn screening, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency

20	## INTRODUCTION
21	
22	1.
23	
24	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) is a rare genetic disease associated with mutations of the ALDH5A1 gene, tissue accumulation of neuromodulators including γ‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) and γ‐hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), and tissue depletion of glutamine (gln), the precursor of GABA and glutamic acid (glu). SSADHD presents with nonspecific mild to moderate developmental delay, intellectual deficiency, severe expressive language impairment, neuropsychiatric problems (ADHD, obsessive compulsive disorder, autistic behavior), and variable epilepsy.1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 There have been reports of sudden unexplained death of epilepsy9, 10 (Gibson, unpublished).
25	
26	Current approaches and major gaps to patient identification and treatment are summarized in Figure 1. Since SSADHD was first described in 1981, research has focused on identifying the spectrum of pathogenic ALDH5A1 mutations, understanding the molecular and biochemical basis of disease presentation, and testing promising therapeutics. The development of an animal model11 resulted in significant strides in elucidation of pathomechanisms and development of novel preclinical therapeutics, including a recently completed interventional trial with the GABA_BR antagonist SGS‐742 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02019667), as well as a completed open‐label trial of taurine which failed to demonstrate efficacy.12 Treatment for SSADHD remains symptomatic, yet an expanding therapeutic preclinical pipeline strongly suggests that targeted and effective therapies (in addition to vigabatrin, which directly targets GABA metabolism) for SSADHD are on the horizon.13
27

VGB (vigabatrin; γ‐vinylGABA; Sabril) represents an irreversible inhibitor of GABA‐T
29	
30	Implementation of newborn screening (NBS) for SSADHD is clinically important for a number of reasons. Expanded NBS would maximize the therapeutic benefit of targeted therapeutics, facilitate family planning, and remove the potential off‐target effects of commonly used symptomatic agents, effectively constituting “treatment by omission.” Further, NBS could synergize with a recently undertaken natural history study of SSADHD through significant expansion of the span of longitudinal assessment of the disorder. NBS would detect patients who will develop milder forms of the disease, or patients with clinical presentations so subtle that they may be misdiagnosed. The potential for delayed diagnosis is highlighted in the postmortem identification of an adult male in the fifth decade.5 Early patient diagnosis would further serve to refine disease prevalence estimates, increase the pool of patients available for a natural history study and future clinical trials, and provide insight on disease pathogenesis and the genetic factors that track with milder disease presentation.
31	
32	The incidence of SSADHD has been estimated at 1 × 10^6 based upon mutation (allele) frequency (Dr Nilah Monnier, Stanford‐personal communication). Mutation analysis has been available for many years.14 Detection of SSADHD has continued to expand with the addition of ALDH5A1 gene analysis to several commercial epilepsy and intellectual disability panels; however, only ~50% of SSADHD patients have seizures, suggesting that many patients remain undiagnosed. On the other hand, methodology for GHB quantitation in dried bloodspots (DBS) has been presented.15 That method utilized liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry (LC‐MS/MS). At least in the United States, only a very limited number of states employ LC/MS‐MS for metabolite quantification, primarily because it is insufficiently high‐throughput (run time 2‐3 minutes per DBS vs 1 minute with MS/MS alone). States with smaller populations, and an often correspondingly lower birthrate, have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS which can expand their metabolic screening “menu,” but states with larger populations (New York, California, and Texas) may only have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS as a second tier screen, or for very specialized analytical needs. Nonetheless, GHB quantitation in DBS represents a very attractive second tier test for confirmation of SSADHD.
33	
34	Recent surveys of SSADHD families worldwide indicate that the median age at disease onset is 1 year whereas the median age at diagnosis is 3 years, that is, a 2‐year delay after the first clinical symptoms. Under current circumstances (with a median age at diagnosis of 3 years), any natural history study of SSADHD would not include patients diagnosed in the early newborn period, representing a major confound from the neurodevelopmental perspective of a disease manifesting a prominent neurological phenotype. Moreover, these survey data provide a measurable perspective on the disease burden for SSADHD families who have to wait 3 years to achieve a diagnosis, as well as the public health and societal impact of delayed diagnosis. To address these unmet healthcare needs, we examined the hypothesis that an integrated screen of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) could be used to potentially identify a metabolomic pattern that could be used as an first‐tier screening tool for SSADHD using DBS, an approach that has been successful in a number of inborn errors of metabolism.16, 17, 18

95	### Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports
96	
97	2.3.
98	
99	Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports (CLIR 2.12; https://clir.mayo.edu) is a web application that maintains an interactive database of laboratory results from multiple sites and provides on demand clinical decision support for their integrated interpretation.25 CLIR replace conventional reference intervals with continuous, covariate‐adjusted moving percentiles,26 as well as replacement of analyte decision limits (ie, cutoff values) with a condition‐specific degree of overlap between reference and disease ranges. Further, an additional feature of CLIR incorporates integration of primary markers and unbiased biomarker discovery by automated calculation of all possible permutations of ratios (A/B) plus manual selection of complex ratios and equations, which can be performed simultaneously for all conditions that can be diagnosed from the available laboratory measurements.

Statistical analysis included one‐way analysis of variance or two‐tailed t test using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (San Diego, California).

183	## DISCUSSION
184	
185	4.
186	
187	### Comparison of metabolic panels to detect SSADHD in DBS
188	
189	4.1.
190	
191	#### Informative amino acid markers
192	
193	4.1.1.
194	
195	Based upon the known metabolic correlations between glutamine, glutamate, and GABA,27, 28, 29 our initial prediction was glutamic acid and glutamine would serve as informative markers for SSADHD in DBS. These amino acids were, however, noninformative, whereas ornithine and histidine were. Indeed, the most consistent amino acid dysregulation was that of ornithine, both in post‐newborn and newborn DBS. Low ornithine has hitherto not been reported in plasma amino acid analysis of patients with SSADHD. Conversely, ornithine has been implicated in the ocular toxicity associated with vigabatrin, an antiepileptic whose mode of action encompasses irreversible inactivation of GABA‐transaminase (Figure 1) with concomitant elevation of GABA, a finding analogous to that of SSADHD.30 Shank and Campbell31 demonstrated that both orn and gln can serve to replenish glu and GABA pools, although gln has a more prominent role in this process.
196	
197	Of interest, histidine was only informative for post‐newborn DBS and not newborn DBS. It is noteworthy that histidine is conjugated with GABA in CNS to derive the dipeptide homocarnosine, an osmoregulator that is also increased in cerebrospinal fluid of SSADHD patients.32, 33 Nevertheless, we could not document the presence of homocarnosine in post‐newborn SSADHD DBS, perhaps indicating that the enzyme required for GABA‐histidine conjugation is not active in the newborn period.

10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractAnalyses of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) were implemented to test the hypothesis that succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) could be identified in dried bloodspots (DBS) using currently available newborn screening methodology. The study population included 17 post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (age range 0.8‐38 years; median, 8.2 years; 10 M; controls, 129‐353 age‐matched individuals, mixed gender) and 10 newborn SSADHD DBS (including first and second screens from 3 of 7 patients). Low (informative) markers in post‐newborn DBS included C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, ornithine, histidine and creatine, with no gender differences. For newborn DBS, informative markers included C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, creatine and ornithine. Of these, only creatine demonstrated a significant change with age, revealing an approximate 4‐fold decrease. We conclude that quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method for γ‐hydroxybutyric acid in the same DBS. More extensive evaluation of this first/second tier screening approach is needed in a larger population.Keywords: acylcarnitines, amino acids, creatine, dried bloodspots, newborn screening, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency

20	## INTRODUCTION
21	
22	1.
23	
24	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) is a rare genetic disease associated with mutations of the ALDH5A1 gene, tissue accumulation of neuromodulators including γ‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) and γ‐hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), and tissue depletion of glutamine (gln), the precursor of GABA and glutamic acid (glu). SSADHD presents with nonspecific mild to moderate developmental delay, intellectual deficiency, severe expressive language impairment, neuropsychiatric problems (ADHD, obsessive compulsive disorder, autistic behavior), and variable epilepsy.1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 There have been reports of sudden unexplained death of epilepsy9, 10 (Gibson, unpublished).
25	
26	Current approaches and major gaps to patient identification and treatment are summarized in Figure 1. Since SSADHD was first described in 1981, research has focused on identifying the spectrum of pathogenic ALDH5A1 mutations, understanding the molecular and biochemical basis of disease presentation, and testing promising therapeutics. The development of an animal model11 resulted in significant strides in elucidation of pathomechanisms and development of novel preclinical therapeutics, including a recently completed interventional trial with the GABA_BR antagonist SGS‐742 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02019667), as well as a completed open‐label trial of taurine which failed to demonstrate efficacy.12 Treatment for SSADHD remains symptomatic, yet an expanding therapeutic preclinical pipeline strongly suggests that targeted and effective therapies (in addition to vigabatrin, which directly targets GABA metabolism) for SSADHD are on the horizon.13
27

VGB (vigabatrin; γ‐vinylGABA; Sabril) represents an irreversible inhibitor of GABA‐T
29	
30	Implementation of newborn screening (NBS) for SSADHD is clinically important for a number of reasons. Expanded NBS would maximize the therapeutic benefit of targeted therapeutics, facilitate family planning, and remove the potential off‐target effects of commonly used symptomatic agents, effectively constituting “treatment by omission.” Further, NBS could synergize with a recently undertaken natural history study of SSADHD through significant expansion of the span of longitudinal assessment of the disorder. NBS would detect patients who will develop milder forms of the disease, or patients with clinical presentations so subtle that they may be misdiagnosed. The potential for delayed diagnosis is highlighted in the postmortem identification of an adult male in the fifth decade.5 Early patient diagnosis would further serve to refine disease prevalence estimates, increase the pool of patients available for a natural history study and future clinical trials, and provide insight on disease pathogenesis and the genetic factors that track with milder disease presentation.
31	
32	The incidence of SSADHD has been estimated at 1 × 10^6 based upon mutation (allele) frequency (Dr Nilah Monnier, Stanford‐personal communication). Mutation analysis has been available for many years.14 Detection of SSADHD has continued to expand with the addition of ALDH5A1 gene analysis to several commercial epilepsy and intellectual disability panels; however, only ~50% of SSADHD patients have seizures, suggesting that many patients remain undiagnosed. On the other hand, methodology for GHB quantitation in dried bloodspots (DBS) has been presented.15 That method utilized liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry (LC‐MS/MS). At least in the United States, only a very limited number of states employ LC/MS‐MS for metabolite quantification, primarily because it is insufficiently high‐throughput (run time 2‐3 minutes per DBS vs 1 minute with MS/MS alone). States with smaller populations, and an often correspondingly lower birthrate, have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS which can expand their metabolic screening “menu,” but states with larger populations (New York, California, and Texas) may only have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS as a second tier screen, or for very specialized analytical needs. Nonetheless, GHB quantitation in DBS represents a very attractive second tier test for confirmation of SSADHD.
33	
34	Recent surveys of SSADHD families worldwide indicate that the median age at disease onset is 1 year whereas the median age at diagnosis is 3 years, that is, a 2‐year delay after the first clinical symptoms. Under current circumstances (with a median age at diagnosis of 3 years), any natural history study of SSADHD would not include patients diagnosed in the early newborn period, representing a major confound from the neurodevelopmental perspective of a disease manifesting a prominent neurological phenotype. Moreover, these survey data provide a measurable perspective on the disease burden for SSADHD families who have to wait 3 years to achieve a diagnosis, as well as the public health and societal impact of delayed diagnosis. To address these unmet healthcare needs, we examined the hypothesis that an integrated screen of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) could be used to potentially identify a metabolomic pattern that could be used as an first‐tier screening tool for SSADHD using DBS, an approach that has been successful in a number of inborn errors of metabolism.16, 17, 18

95	### Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports
96	
97	2.3.
98	
99	Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports (CLIR 2.12; https://clir.mayo.edu) is a web application that maintains an interactive database of laboratory results from multiple sites and provides on demand clinical decision support for their integrated interpretation.25 CLIR replace conventional reference intervals with continuous, covariate‐adjusted moving percentiles,26 as well as replacement of analyte decision limits (ie, cutoff values) with a condition‐specific degree of overlap between reference and disease ranges. Further, an additional feature of CLIR incorporates integration of primary markers and unbiased biomarker discovery by automated calculation of all possible permutations of ratios (A/B) plus manual selection of complex ratios and equations, which can be performed simultaneously for all conditions that can be diagnosed from the available laboratory measurements.

Statistical analysis included one‐way analysis of variance or two‐tailed t test using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (San Diego, California).

183	## DISCUSSION
184	
185	4.
186	
187	### Comparison of metabolic panels to detect SSADHD in DBS
188	
189	4.1.
190	
191	#### Informative amino acid markers
192	
193	4.1.1.
194	
195	Based upon the known metabolic correlations between glutamine, glutamate, and GABA,27, 28, 29 our initial prediction was glutamic acid and glutamine would serve as informative markers for SSADHD in DBS. These amino acids were, however, noninformative, whereas ornithine and histidine were. Indeed, the most consistent amino acid dysregulation was that of ornithine, both in post‐newborn and newborn DBS. Low ornithine has hitherto not been reported in plasma amino acid analysis of patients with SSADHD. Conversely, ornithine has been implicated in the ocular toxicity associated with vigabatrin, an antiepileptic whose mode of action encompasses irreversible inactivation of GABA‐transaminase (Figure 1) with concomitant elevation of GABA, a finding analogous to that of SSADHD.30 Shank and Campbell31 demonstrated that both orn and gln can serve to replenish glu and GABA pools, although gln has a more prominent role in this process.
196	
197	Of interest, histidine was only informative for post‐newborn DBS and not newborn DBS. It is noteworthy that histidine is conjugated with GABA in CNS to derive the dipeptide homocarnosine, an osmoregulator that is also increased in cerebrospinal fluid of SSADHD patients.32, 33 Nevertheless, we could not document the presence of homocarnosine in post‐newborn SSADHD DBS, perhaps indicating that the enzyme required for GABA‐histidine conjugation is not active in the newborn period.

10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractAnalyses of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) were implemented to test the hypothesis that succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) could be identified in dried bloodspots (DBS) using currently available newborn screening methodology. The study population included 17 post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (age range 0.8‐38 years; median, 8.2 years; 10 M; controls, 129‐353 age‐matched individuals, mixed gender) and 10 newborn SSADHD DBS (including first and second screens from 3 of 7 patients). Low (informative) markers in post‐newborn DBS included C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, ornithine, histidine and creatine, with no gender differences. For newborn DBS, informative markers included C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, creatine and ornithine. Of these, only creatine demonstrated a significant change with age, revealing an approximate 4‐fold decrease. We conclude that quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method for γ‐hydroxybutyric acid in the same DBS. More extensive evaluation of this first/second tier screening approach is needed in a larger population.Keywords: acylcarnitines, amino acids, creatine, dried bloodspots, newborn screening, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency

20	## INTRODUCTION
21	
22	1.
23	
24	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) is a rare genetic disease associated with mutations of the ALDH5A1 gene, tissue accumulation of neuromodulators including γ‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) and γ‐hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), and tissue depletion of glutamine (gln), the precursor of GABA and glutamic acid (glu). SSADHD presents with nonspecific mild to moderate developmental delay, intellectual deficiency, severe expressive language impairment, neuropsychiatric problems (ADHD, obsessive compulsive disorder, autistic behavior), and variable epilepsy.1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 There have been reports of sudden unexplained death of epilepsy9, 10 (Gibson, unpublished).
25	
26	Current approaches and major gaps to patient identification and treatment are summarized in Figure 1. Since SSADHD was first described in 1981, research has focused on identifying the spectrum of pathogenic ALDH5A1 mutations, understanding the molecular and biochemical basis of disease presentation, and testing promising therapeutics. The development of an animal model11 resulted in significant strides in elucidation of pathomechanisms and development of novel preclinical therapeutics, including a recently completed interventional trial with the GABA_BR antagonist SGS‐742 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02019667), as well as a completed open‐label trial of taurine which failed to demonstrate efficacy.12 Treatment for SSADHD remains symptomatic, yet an expanding therapeutic preclinical pipeline strongly suggests that targeted and effective therapies (in addition to vigabatrin, which directly targets GABA metabolism) for SSADHD are on the horizon.13
27

VGB (vigabatrin; γ‐vinylGABA; Sabril) represents an irreversible inhibitor of GABA‐T
29	
30	Implementation of newborn screening (NBS) for SSADHD is clinically important for a number of reasons. Expanded NBS would maximize the therapeutic benefit of targeted therapeutics, facilitate family planning, and remove the potential off‐target effects of commonly used symptomatic agents, effectively constituting “treatment by omission.” Further, NBS could synergize with a recently undertaken natural history study of SSADHD through significant expansion of the span of longitudinal assessment of the disorder. NBS would detect patients who will develop milder forms of the disease, or patients with clinical presentations so subtle that they may be misdiagnosed. The potential for delayed diagnosis is highlighted in the postmortem identification of an adult male in the fifth decade.5 Early patient diagnosis would further serve to refine disease prevalence estimates, increase the pool of patients available for a natural history study and future clinical trials, and provide insight on disease pathogenesis and the genetic factors that track with milder disease presentation.
31	
32	The incidence of SSADHD has been estimated at 1 × 10^6 based upon mutation (allele) frequency (Dr Nilah Monnier, Stanford‐personal communication). Mutation analysis has been available for many years.14 Detection of SSADHD has continued to expand with the addition of ALDH5A1 gene analysis to several commercial epilepsy and intellectual disability panels; however, only ~50% of SSADHD patients have seizures, suggesting that many patients remain undiagnosed. On the other hand, methodology for GHB quantitation in dried bloodspots (DBS) has been presented.15 That method utilized liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry (LC‐MS/MS). At least in the United States, only a very limited number of states employ LC/MS‐MS for metabolite quantification, primarily because it is insufficiently high‐throughput (run time 2‐3 minutes per DBS vs 1 minute with MS/MS alone). States with smaller populations, and an often correspondingly lower birthrate, have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS which can expand their metabolic screening “menu,” but states with larger populations (New York, California, and Texas) may only have the capacity to employ LC‐MS/MS as a second tier screen, or for very specialized analytical needs. Nonetheless, GHB quantitation in DBS represents a very attractive second tier test for confirmation of SSADHD.
33	
34	Recent surveys of SSADHD families worldwide indicate that the median age at disease onset is 1 year whereas the median age at diagnosis is 3 years, that is, a 2‐year delay after the first clinical symptoms. Under current circumstances (with a median age at diagnosis of 3 years), any natural history study of SSADHD would not include patients diagnosed in the early newborn period, representing a major confound from the neurodevelopmental perspective of a disease manifesting a prominent neurological phenotype. Moreover, these survey data provide a measurable perspective on the disease burden for SSADHD families who have to wait 3 years to achieve a diagnosis, as well as the public health and societal impact of delayed diagnosis. To address these unmet healthcare needs, we examined the hypothesis that an integrated screen of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) could be used to potentially identify a metabolomic pattern that could be used as an first‐tier screening tool for SSADHD using DBS, an approach that has been successful in a number of inborn errors of metabolism.16, 17, 18

95	### Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports
96	
97	2.3.
98	
99	Collaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports (CLIR 2.12; https://clir.mayo.edu) is a web application that maintains an interactive database of laboratory results from multiple sites and provides on demand clinical decision support for their integrated interpretation.25 CLIR replace conventional reference intervals with continuous, covariate‐adjusted moving percentiles,26 as well as replacement of analyte decision limits (ie, cutoff values) with a condition‐specific degree of overlap between reference and disease ranges. Further, an additional feature of CLIR incorporates integration of primary markers and unbiased biomarker discovery by automated calculation of all possible permutations of ratios (A/B) plus manual selection of complex ratios and equations, which can be performed simultaneously for all conditions that can be diagnosed from the available laboratory measurements.

Statistical analysis included one‐way analysis of variance or two‐tailed t test using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (San Diego, California).

183	## DISCUSSION
184	
185	4.
186	
187	### Comparison of metabolic panels to detect SSADHD in DBS
188	
189	4.1.
190	
191	#### Informative amino acid markers
192	
193	4.1.1.
194	
195	Based upon the known metabolic correlations between glutamine, glutamate, and GABA,27, 28, 29 our initial prediction was glutamic acid and glutamine would serve as informative markers for SSADHD in DBS. These amino acids were, however, noninformative, whereas ornithine and histidine were. Indeed, the most consistent amino acid dysregulation was that of ornithine, both in post‐newborn and newborn DBS. Low ornithine has hitherto not been reported in plasma amino acid analysis of patients with SSADHD. Conversely, ornithine has been implicated in the ocular toxicity associated with vigabatrin, an antiepileptic whose mode of action encompasses irreversible inactivation of GABA‐transaminase (Figure 1) with concomitant elevation of GABA, a finding analogous to that of SSADHD.30 Shank and Campbell31 demonstrated that both orn and gln can serve to replenish glu and GABA pools, although gln has a more prominent role in this process.
196	
197	Of interest, histidine was only informative for post‐newborn DBS and not newborn DBS. It is noteworthy that histidine is conjugated with GABA in CNS to derive the dipeptide homocarnosine, an osmoregulator that is also increased in cerebrospinal fluid of SSADHD patients.32, 33 Nevertheless, we could not document the presence of homocarnosine in post‐newborn SSADHD DBS, perhaps indicating that the enzyme required for GABA‐histidine conjugation is not active in the newborn period.

10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractAnalyses of 19 amino acids, 38 acylcarnitines, and 3 creatine analogues (https://clir.mayo.edu) were implemented to test the hypothesis that succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADHD) could be identified in dried bloodspots (DBS) using currently available newborn screening methodology. The study population included 17 post‐newborn SSADHD DBS (age range 0.8‐38 years; median, 8.2 years; 10 M; controls, 129‐353 age‐matched individuals, mixed gender) and 10 newborn SSADHD DBS (including first and second screens from 3 of 7 patients). Low (informative) markers in post‐newborn DBS included C2‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, ornithine, histidine and creatine, with no gender differences. For newborn DBS, informative markers included C2‐, C3‐, C4‐ and C4‐OH carnitines, creatine and ornithine. Of these, only creatine demonstrated a significant change with age, revealing an approximate 4‐fold decrease. We conclude that quantitation of short‐chain acylcarnitines, creatine, and ornithine provides a newborn DBS profile with potential as a first tier screening tool for early detection of SSADHD. This first tier evaluation can be readily verified using a previously described second tier liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method for γ‐hydroxybutyric acid in the same DBS. More extensive evaluation of this first/second tier screening approach is needed in a larger population.Keywords: acylcarnitines, amino acids, creatine, dried bloodspots, newborn screening, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
